justice: The lane is almost entirely allocated to a narrow shared carriageway, with no dedicated sidewalk or protected space for pedestrians and cyclists.
The waterside edge on the left lacks a visible guardrail or continuous barrier, creating unequal risk exposure for users traveling close to the canal.
No curb ramps, tactile paving, or other barrier-free elements are visible, so accessibility support is minimal for users with diverse mobility needs.
safety: The road is extremely narrow, forcing any pedestrians, cyclists, and motor vehicles to mix in the same space with little room to avoid conflicts.
An open waterbody runs directly along the left side of the lane, and the edge protection appears discontinuous or absent in several places.
Leaning utility poles and low overhead wires along the route suggest infrastructure hazards and reduce perceived safety.
livability: The street lacks visible public amenities such as benches, shops, lighting fixtures, or gathering spaces that would support daily social life.
Blank compound walls on the right and fenced edges on the left create a corridor-like environment with limited active frontage.
Scattered debris and construction materials near the foreground reduce environmental quality and make the setting feel less supportive for everyday use.
sustainability: The presence of a tree and adjacent waterbody adds some ecological value and minor landscape cooling potential.
There is little visible green infrastructure such as street trees, bioswales, permeable planting strips, or organized stormwater features along the lane.
The narrow lane may limit high-speed car use, but there is no dedicated walking or cycling infrastructure to clearly support low-carbon transport.
aesthetics: The canal and vegetation provide some natural scenery and visual openness on the left side of the image.
However, exposed wires, leaning poles, and patched pavement create visual disorder and weaken the overall streetscape quality.
Plain wall surfaces with large painted numbers and visible clutter along the edge reduce visual coherence and refinement.
comfort: There is very limited shade over the lane, with only sparse tree cover, so thermal comfort is likely poor in hot weather.
The roadway surface shows patching and edge irregularities, which can reduce physical comfort for walking, cycling, and driving.
The narrow enclosed lane beside a blank wall on one side and open water on the other may create psychological discomfort because of constrained movement space and edge risk.
walkability: No continuous sidewalk is visible, so pedestrians must walk directly on the vehicular surface.
The lane is narrow and bordered by a wall on one side and canal edge on the other, leaving little refuge or passing space for walkers.
Surface patching, roadside debris, and the absence of crossings, wayfinding, or pedestrian buffers make walking less convenient and less attractive.
bikeability: There is no marked or protected bike lane, so cyclists would need to share the very narrow road with motor vehicles.
The patched pavement and tight edge conditions near the canal increase instability and perceived crash risk for cycling.
Lack of lane markings, buffers, and bicycle parking indicates little infrastructure support for everyday bike use.
